title: Working Drawings & Conventions
description: 2D engineering drawings using third-angle orthographic projection — BS 8888 conventions, title blocks, scale.
content_html:
What Is a Working Drawing?

A working drawing is the definitive document from which a component or assembly is manufactured. It must be complete, unambiguous and fully standardised so that any qualified engineer or machinist — anywhere in the world — can interpret it correctly. In the UK, working drawings follow the conventions set out in BS 8888 (Technical product documentation). The standard covers everything from the layout of the title block to the way a diameter dimension is written.

Third-Angle Orthographic Projection

All working drawings in the UK use third-angle orthographic projection. The object is imagined placed inside a transparent glass box. Each face of the box is a projection plane: the view from the front is projected onto the front plane, the view from the top is projected onto the top plane, and the view from the right is projected onto the right plane. When the box is unfolded, the standard arrangement places the front view (elevation) in the centre, the plan (top view) above it, and the right end view to its right. The internationally recognised symbol for third-angle projection — a truncated cone seen from the narrow end — must appear in the title block of every working drawing to confirm which standard is used.

Key Fact

In third-angle orthographic projection (standard in the UK), the plan view is placed above the front view and the right end view is placed to the right of the front view. The symbol is a truncated cone viewed from its narrow end.

The Title Block and Standard Conventions

Every engineering drawing has a title block, typically in the bottom-right corner. It contains the drawing title, drawing number, designer's name, date, scale, sheet size, material, finish, projection symbol and revision history. The title block ensures traceability — if a component is made incorrectly, the drawing can be traced back to the person who produced it and the revision that was current at the time. All measurements on a working drawing are in metric units (millimetres unless otherwise stated). The scale used must be stated clearly — for example, 1:1 (full size), 2:1 (twice full size), or 1:5 (one fifth full size). Drawing to scale allows the viewer to check proportions visually.

Dimensioning Conventions

Dimensions are added using dimension lines, projection lines and leader lines, all drawn as thin continuous lines. Dimension lines run parallel to the feature being measured, with arrowheads touching projection lines that extend just beyond the outline of the part. The dimension value is placed above or in a gap in the dimension line. Linear measurements give the straight-line distance between two points. Radii are written with the prefix R (e.g., R12); diameters are written with the prefix ⌀ (the Greek letter phi) or the abbreviation DIA. Surface finish requirements — how smooth a surface must be — are shown using the surface texture symbol. A square cross-section is indicated by the abbreviation SQ or the □ symbol before the dimension value. Standard abbreviations used on drawings include: AF (across flats), CL or ℄ (centre line), DIA or ⌀ (diameter), DRG (drawing), MATL (material), SQ (square).

BS 8888 defines six line types that every drawing must use correctly. Outlines (continuous thick lines) show visible edges and contours of the object. Hidden detail lines (short dashes, thin) show edges and surfaces that are behind other features and cannot be seen in that view. Centre lines (thin chain — alternating long and short dashes) mark the axes of symmetry, circles and cylindrical features. Projection lines (thin continuous) extend from the outline to indicate where a dimension applies but do not touch the outline. Dimension lines (thin continuous with arrowheads) carry the dimension value. Leader lines (thin continuous with arrowhead or dot) point from a note or symbol to the feature it refers to. Confusing outline and hidden detail lines is one of the most common errors in exam drawing questions.

Key Fact

The six line types in BS 8888 are: outlines (thick continuous), hidden detail (thin dashes), centre lines (thin chain — long-short dash), projection lines (thin continuous), dimension lines (thin continuous with arrowheads), and leader lines (thin continuous with arrowhead or dot).

Tolerances

No machining process is perfectly precise. A tolerance specifies the permissible variation in a dimension — for example, a shaft might be dimensioned as ⌀25 +0.02/−0.01 mm, meaning the diameter must be between 24.99 mm and 25.02 mm. Tolerances are essential for ensuring interchangeability of parts in mass production: if every component is made within its tolerance, any shaft will fit any matching hole without selective fitting. Tighter tolerances require more precise (and more expensive) machining processes. The designer must balance functional requirements against manufacturing cost when specifying tolerances.

Representing Mechanical Features

Some features have standard drawing conventions because they cannot be drawn realistically at small scale. External and internal threads are shown using thick outlines for the crest of the thread and thin lines for the root, with a cross-hatching convention visible in section views. Holes are shown in plan as circles and in elevation with centre lines. Chamfers (angled cuts at the end of a shaft or hole edge) are shown with angled lines at the relevant corner. Countersinks (conical enlargements at the entrance of a hole) are shown with a cone symbol in the elevation view. Knurls (textured grip patterns on a cylindrical surface) are shown with a cross-hatched pattern on the surface.

Examiners regularly see the same mistakes in working drawing questions. First, omitting the third-angle projection symbol from the title block. Second, placing the plan view below the front view instead of above it (that is first-angle, used in mainland Europe). Third, using a continuous thick line for hidden detail (it should be short dashes, thin). Fourth, writing dimensions in inches or mixing units. Fifth, omitting tolerances on a critical dimension when the question states that the component must fit a mating part. Practise producing complete, correctly labelled working drawings including the title block to avoid these errors.
exam_tip_html: If an exam question asks you to add dimensions or line types to a drawing, always label dimensions with arrowheads on thin dimension lines separated from the outline by thin projection lines, never by touching the outline. State radii with R and diameters with ⌀. If the question asks which projection standard is used in the UK, the answer is third-angle orthographic projection — and remember that first-angle (used in Europe) places the plan below the front view, which is the opposite of third-angle.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Working drawings in the UK follow BS 8888 and use third-angle orthographic projection, in which the plan is above the front view and the right end view is to the right — the projection symbol (truncated cone) must appear in the title block.
  • Six line types define what every element of an engineering drawing communicates — outlines (thick continuous), hidden detail (thin dashes), centre lines (thin chain), projection lines (thin continuous), dimension lines (thin continuous with arrowheads), and leader lines.
  • Tolerances specify the permissible variation in a dimension, balancing functional requirements against manufacturing cost, and are essential for ensuring parts are interchangeable in mass production.

glossary_terms.definition: A fully dimensioned, annotated 2D engineering drawing produced to a standard that allows a component to be manufactured without further information.
The British Standard for technical product documentation, specifying drawing conventions, line types, dimensioning and tolerancing rules used in UK engineering drawings.
A drawing method in which each view is projected onto the face of a glass box nearest to the viewer, placing the plan above the front view and the right end view to the right.
The permissible range of variation in a dimension, stated as an upper and lower limit, within which a manufactured component will still function correctly.

practice_questions.text:
In a UK third-angle orthographic drawing, where is the plan view positioned relative to the front view?
A) Below the front view
B) To the left of the front view
C) Above the front view
D) To the right of the front view
practice_questions.marks: C) Above the front view [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two items of information that must be included in the title block of an engineering drawing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: drawing title / drawing number / designer's name / date / scale / sheet size / material / finish / projection symbol / revision history. Accept any two clearly different items. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a hidden detail line and an outline on an engineering drawing.
practice_questions.marks: Outline (1 mark): a continuous thick line showing visible edges of the object. Hidden detail (1 mark): a thin dashed line showing edges or surfaces that are hidden behind other features in that view. Development (1 mark): for example, if a blind hole is drilled into a block, the bottom of the hole cannot be seen in the front view, so it is shown as a thin dashed line to indicate its presence without it being visible. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by a tolerance on an engineering drawing. Give one example of why tolerances are important in manufacturing.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a tolerance is the permissible range of variation in a manufactured dimension, stated as an upper and lower limit; for example ⌀25 +0.02/−0.01 mm means the diameter must be between 24.99 mm and 25.02 mm (2 marks for a developed description including both upper and lower limits; 1 mark for a basic statement such as 'it shows how much a dimension can vary'). Example (up to 2 marks): tolerances ensure that components are interchangeable — in mass production, if every shaft is made within its tolerance, it will fit any matching bearing without selective assembly, reducing production costs and assembly time (2 marks for a specific example; 1 mark for a vague point about accuracy). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A student is producing a working drawing of a machined shaft that includes a threaded section, a knurled grip and a chamfered end. The shaft must fit a matching bearing with an interference fit.

Discuss the drawing conventions and information that the student must include to communicate this component fully to a manufacturer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced response that addresses at least three of the following with explanation: third-angle orthographic projection with the correct projection symbol in the title block; correct line types (outlines, hidden detail, centre lines, dimension lines, projection lines); dimensioning of the thread using the standard thread convention (thick and thin lines, root and crest); the knurl shown with cross-hatched pattern; the chamfer shown with an angled line and dimensioned angle or linear value; a tolerance on the bearing diameter to specify the interference fit. Both the choice of convention and the reason for its importance are addressed.
Secure (3–4 marks): At least two conventions identified with some explanation but limited development or missing the tolerance point.
Developing (2 marks): One or two conventions identified with minimal explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A basic relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A manufacturing company uses working drawings conforming to BS 8888 to produce components that are assembled at different factories across the UK.

Evaluate the importance of using standardised drawing conventions when communicating engineering designs for manufacture.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation identifying the strong arguments for standardisation — unambiguous communication meaning any engineer can interpret the drawing correctly; interchangeability of parts because tolerances are understood consistently; legal traceability through the title block; reduced risk of manufacturing errors and costly rework — then genuinely challenging these with counterpoints, such as the initial cost and time of training all engineers to the standard, the cost of drawing software that enforces BS 8888, and the fact that for one-off prototype work informal sketches may be faster and perfectly adequate. A clear judgement is reached — for example, that standardisation is essential for production components where accuracy and interchangeability matter, but proportionality is needed and one-off prototyping can use less formal approaches.
Secure (5–6 marks): Strengths and limitations identified with some development and an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Largely one-sided, focusing only on advantages with limited or no counterargument.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points about standardisation with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: In third-angle orthographic projection (UK standard), where is the plan view positioned?
options: To the right of the front view
To the left of the front view

knowledge_checks.q: Which British Standard specifies the conventions used in UK engineering working drawings?
Hidden detail lines on an engineering drawing are drawn as _____ lines.
The abbreviation ⌀ (phi) on an engineering drawing indicates a _____.
Match each line type to its correct description.
right: Thin continuous line with arrowheads; carries the dimension value
Thick continuous line showing visible edges of the object
Thin chain (long-short dash) marking axes of symmetry or cylindrical features

flashcard_questions.q: What is the standard orthographic projection used in UK working drawings?
flashcard_questions.a: Third-angle orthographic projection is the standard used in the UK, as specified by BS 8888.

flashcard_questions.q: In third-angle projection, where is the plan view positioned relative to the front view?
flashcard_questions.a: The plan view is positioned above the front view, and the right end view is positioned to the right of the front view.

flashcard_questions.q: What symbol is used to indicate third-angle projection on a drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: A truncated cone viewed from its narrow end is the internationally recognised symbol for third-angle orthographic projection.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a tolerance on an engineering drawing specify?
flashcard_questions.a: A tolerance specifies the permissible range of variation in a dimension — the upper and lower limits within which a manufactured component will still function correctly.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the purpose of a title block on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: The title block records key information including drawing title, number, scale, material, projection symbol and revision history, ensuring the drawing is fully traceable.

flashcard_questions.q: What line type is used for hidden detail on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: Hidden detail is shown using thin dashed lines, indicating edges or surfaces that are hidden behind other features in that particular view.

flashcard_questions.q: What line type is used for centre lines on a drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: Centre lines are drawn as thin chain lines — alternating long and short dashes — to mark axes of symmetry and the centres of circles or cylindrical features.

flashcard_questions.q: How is a diameter dimension written on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: A diameter dimension is written using the ⌀ symbol (or the abbreviation DIA) before the numerical value, for example ⌀25 mm.

flashcard_questions.q: How is a radius dimension written on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: A radius dimension is written using the prefix R before the numerical value, for example R12 mm, and the dimension line points to the arc with a single arrowhead.

flashcard_questions.q: What does the abbreviation AF mean on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: AF stands for across flats, indicating the distance measured across the parallel flat faces of a hexagonal or square feature such as a bolt head.

flashcard_questions.q: How are external threads represented on an engineering drawing?
flashcard_questions.a: External threads are shown with thick continuous lines for the crest of the thread and thin continuous lines for the root, with a specific cross-hatching convention used in section views.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are tolerances essential in mass production?
flashcard_questions.a: Tolerances ensure that components are interchangeable — any part made within its specified limits will fit a mating part correctly without selective assembly, reducing manufacturing cost and assembly time.
